'''''Plectranthus verticillatus''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Plectranthus nummularius''<ref>cf. ''theplantlist.org'': [http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl/record/kew-158353 Plectranthus verticillatus (L.f.) Druce]. Retrieved 13 February 2013.</ref>), '''Swedish ivy''', '''Swedish begonia''' or '''whorled plectranthus'''<ref name=weeds>{{cite web|url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/03030800-0b07-490a-8d04-0605030c0f01/media/Html/Plectranthus_verticillatus.htm|title=Swedish ivy Plectranthus verticillatus|work=Weeds of Australia|publisher=University of Queensland|access-date=14 February 2013}}</ref> is a plant in the family [[Lamiaceae]] (Labiatae), genus ''[[Plectranthus]]'' native to [[southern Africa]]. Despite its common name, it is not close to the ivy family of the genus ''[[Hedera]]'' nor is it native to [[Sweden]].

==Description==
The plant has aromatic glossy, green, round [[Leaf|leaves]], which show a deep purple color in the center sometimes and tend to trail, reaching a height of between 10 and 30 cm and extends around 60 cm. This deep purple can also be found on the [[plant stem]]s and on the underside of leaves. The leaves, which are widely serrated, are fleshy and rounded between 64 and 90 mm, with purple and hairy undersides with reddish [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] glands.

The upright [[raceme]]s appear white, pale violet or pale pink and can sprout sporadically throughout the year (but more typically in spring and late autumn), which form verticillasters of 2-4 flowers and 2–3 mm [[bract]]s. The fruits are 1 mm nuts, brown in colour and wrinkled.<ref>cf. Description and picture at ''PlantZAfrica.com'': [http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantnop/plectranvert.htm Plectranthus verticillatus (L.f.) Druce]. Retrieved 13 February 2013.</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.plantbook.co.za/plectranthus-verticillatus/|title=Plectranthus verticillatus {{!}} Money Plant, Gossip {{!}} PLANTBOOK|date=2015-04-07|work=PLANTBOOK|access-date=2017-07-20|language=en-GB}}</ref>

The name "Swedish ivy" is deceptive: the plant is not [[thigmotropic]] (meaning it does not cling to walls with the roots when it grows), is not native to Sweden, and is not closely related to the genus of [[ivy]] (''Hedera''). Some variegated, silvery plants called Swedish ivy grown in pots and hanging baskets are ''[[Plectranthus oertendahlii]] ''from coastal river gorges of KwaZulu-Natal.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://pza.sanbi.org/plectranthus-verticillatus|title=Plectranthus verticillatus {{!}} PlantZAfrica.com|website=pza.sanbi.org|access-date=2017-07-20}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Plectranthus verticillatus'' is native to [[southern Africa]] where it occurs in the [[Cape Provinces]], [[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Swaziland|Eswatini]], the [[Transvaal Province|Northern Provinces]] and southern [[Mozambique]].<ref name=WCSP>cf. ''World Checklist of Selected Plant Families'': [http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=158574 Plectranthus verticillatus_id=158574]. Retrieved 13 February 2013.</ref> It is found naturalized in [[El Salvador]], [[Honduras]], the [[Leeward Islands]], the [[Federal Dependencies of Venezuela|Venezuela Antilles]], the [[Windward Islands]], [[Venezuela]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Hawaii]] as well as south-east [[Queensland]] and coastal areas of [[New South Wales]] in [[Australia]].<ref name=weeds/><ref name=WCSP/><ref name=NSW>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Plectranthus~verticillatus |title=''Plectranthus verticillatus'' (L.f.) Druce  |access-date=14 February 2013 |author=Conn, B.J.|work= PlantNET - New South Wales Flora Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia}}</ref>

==Use as ornamental plant==
''Plectranthus verticillatus'' is a robust plant doing well in indirect sunlight, mostly cultivated as hanging [[houseplant]]. In frost-free areas, it is also found as [[groundcover]] in gardens or sprouting down walls.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.guide-to-houseplants.com/swedish-ivy.html|title=Swedish Ivy Plant Care - Plectranthus species|access-date=2017-07-20}}</ref> It can tolerate milder frosts if it is grown under a canopy of trees and shrubs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.igarden.com.au/plant-type.jsp?t=plectranthus&id=199|title=Plectranthus verticillatus - Planting, growing and propagating information from iGarden|website=www.igarden.com.au|access-date=2017-07-20}}</ref> Since it is a tender perennial, it is hardy to [[USDA zone]]s 10-11. In cooler climates, it is grown as an indoor [[houseplant]] or as an [[Annual plant|annual]].<ref>[https://www.gardenia.net/plant/plectranthus-verticillatus-swedish-ivy-grow-care-guide Plectranthus verticillatus (Swedish Ivy)] by Gardenia.net. Retrieved 14 April, 2024.</ref>

It likes to stay moist and it also responds well to pruning. It can easily be rooted with [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]] and its vulnerability is low; but a weak plant can be infested with [[spider mite]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/plant.asp?code=B648|title=Plectranthus australis|website=www.mobot.org|access-date=2017-07-20}}</ref>

===US White House===
A [[Oval Office Swedish ivy|notable specimen of ''Plectranthus verticillatus'']] was long to be found above the mantel in the President of the United States' [[Oval Office]]. Though a popular story attributes its origins as a gift to President [[John F. Kennedy]] in 1961, the exact origins are unknown. It had been photographed in every administration since its appearance until it was removed by [[Donald Trump]] in 2025 and replaced with a series of gold objects.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/power/2025/03/18/oval-office-swedish-ivy-obama-plant-trump-missing-kennedy-gold-mantel/|newspaper=[[Washington Post]]|first=Maura|last=Judkis|title=The growing legend of the missing Oval Office ivy|date=18 March 2025|access-date=18 March 2025}}</ref> Interns, aides, and other White House workers are often granted clippings of the famous plant which they grow and further distribute to friends and family.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://denverite.com/2020/04/16/houseplant-of-the-week-the-worlds-most-powerful-plant/|title=Living: Houseplant of the week: The world's most powerful plant|website=denverite.com|date=16 April 2020 |access-date=2021-07-28}}</ref>
